ch02.note: By old convention an educated Chinese man received, on reaching adulthood, a zi (字) or 'courtesy name' by which equals and juniors addressed him; using his given name to his face was a familiarity reserved for elders. Chen names many figures this way. Dai Li's given name was Chunfeng, his courtesy name Yunong.

Like Shanghai, the treaty port of Tianjin was carved into several foreign concessions—British, French, Japanese, and others—each a self-governing enclave outside Chinese jurisdiction. Fugitives, deposed warlords, and enemy agents sheltered in them precisely because Chinese police could not follow, which is why so many of these operations had to be run, at great risk, on concession ground.

The Northwest Army (西北军), the large but chronically underfunded warlord army built up in the 1920s by Feng Yuxiang. After its defeat in the wars of 1929–30 its generals scattered into shifting allegiances; several of the men in this book—Ji Hongchang, Shi Yousan among them—were Northwest Army officers cast loose in that dispersal.

ch02.anchor: the plum tree withered in the peach tree's place
ch02.note: A set image, li dai tao jiang (李代桃僵), 'the plum stands stiff in the peach tree's place': from a Han ballad in which the plum by the well dies of the worms gnawing the peach's roots, one tree perishing for another. Listed as the eleventh of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, it means a substitute taking the blow meant for someone else—here the wrong man, Liu Shaorang, shot down in place of the target.

Dairen (Japanese reading of 大連, now Dalian), the port at the tip of the Liaodong peninsula, held by Japan from 1905 as part of the Kwantung Leased Territory. Being Japanese-controlled ground close to North China, it was a natural base and bolt-hole for men working with or for the Japanese.

A rōnin (浪人) was originally a masterless samurai; by extension a drifter or freelance adventurer. The 'continental rōnin' (大陸浪人) were Japanese adventurers who roamed China in the early twentieth century as traders, spies, fixers, and provocateurs, often doing the army's unofficial work, as Chen says this Yamamoto did.

ch02.anchor: give up his life for righteousness
ch02.note: An allusion to Mencius: 'I like life, and I also like righteousness; if I cannot keep both, I will let life go and choose righteousness' (Mencius 6A.10). Paired in Chinese with the Confucian 'die to complete one's virtue' glossed at the foreword, it is the classic formula for a worthy death—which Chen, setting enmity aside, half-grants even to his enemy.
